title: Stories for Children and Families
intro: Retellings with a short version, a longer version, and a source note. Regional variants are named rather than flattened, and the source note says whether a story is scriptural, Puranic, or regional.
editorialNote: Editorial content authored for this app. It has not been through independent scholarly review. See the Content Verification page.

stories.title: Sati and the Sacred Places
stories.short: Long ago there was a queen called Sati. Her father, Daksha, held a huge fire ceremony and did not invite her husband Shiva, because he did not like him. Sati went anyway. At the ceremony her father insulted Shiva in front of everyone. Sati could not bear it, and she gave up her life in the fire. When Shiva heard, his sadness was so big that he began to dance, and the whole world shook. The other gods were frightened. Vishnu used his spinning disc to cut Sati's body into pieces so the dancing would stop. Every place a piece fell became a holy place. Those places are called Shakti Peethas, and people still visit them today.
stories.long:
Sati was the daughter of Daksha Prajapati. She married Shiva against her father's wishes, because she saw in him what others did not: that his poverty was a choice and his stillness was not emptiness.

Years later Daksha held a great yajna, a fire sacrifice, and invited every important being in the universe except Shiva. Sati argued that a daughter needs no invitation to her father's house, and she went.

She was wrong. Daksha received everyone else with honour and mocked Shiva openly. Sati defended her husband, and was mocked too. At last she understood that staying would only add to the insult, and she entered the sacrificial fire and gave up her body.

When Shiva learned what had happened, his grief took the form of the tandava, a dance of destruction that shook the three worlds. The gods could not stop him. Vishnu, to save the world, used his sudarshana chakra to cut the body Sati had carried into pieces, which fell across the land. Where they fell, the places became sacred — the Shakti Peethas.

Shiva's dance slowed, and in time he was brought back. Later tradition says Sati was born again as Parvati, daughter of the mountain, and won Shiva again.

Different texts list different numbers of Peethas — 18, 51, 52, 64 or 108 — and they do not agree about which part fell where. That disagreement is old and it is honest. The places are real; the list is a matter of tradition.
stories.moral: Grief can become a sacred place. What we cannot bear does not have to be wasted.
stories.sourceNote: Puranic narrative (Kalika Purana, Devi Bhagavata and others). Not part of the Devi Mahatmya. Regional versions differ in detail.

stories.title: Durga and Mahishasura
stories.short: There was a demon called Mahishasura who prayed for so long that the gods had to give him a wish. He asked that no man and no animal could ever kill him. He thought that made him safe forever. He took over heaven and threw the gods out. The gods were desperate. All their anger and all their light came together and became one being: a goddess riding a lion. Mahishasura laughed when he saw her. He did not laugh for long. She fought him, and when he changed shape to escape, she followed. At the end she pinned him down with her foot and killed him with her trident. That victory is why we celebrate Vijayadashami.
stories.long:
Mahishasura was an asura who performed austerities for thousands of years. Brahma finally appeared and offered him a boon. Mahishasura asked for immortality, which even Brahma could not grant, so he settled for the next best thing: that neither a man nor an animal could kill him.

He did not think to mention women. It did not occur to him that it could matter.

With that protection he conquered the three worlds. Indra and the devas were driven out of heaven and wandered the earth like beggars. They went to Vishnu and to Shiva, and from all of them together a great light arose. The light took form, and every god gave her his own weapon: Shiva his trident, Vishnu his discus, Varuna his conch, Agni his spear, Vayu his bow. The mountain gave her a lion to ride.

When Mahishasura's army saw her they attacked. The Devi Mahatmya describes the battle at length — the generals Chikshura and Chamara, the elephants, the showers of weapons. She destroyed the army.

Then Mahishasura came himself, in the form of a great buffalo. He shook the earth with his horns and threw mountains. When she pressed him he changed shape — into a lion, then a man with a sword, then a great elephant — and each time she met him. At last she pinned him under her foot, and as he emerged half-transformed she took his head with the trident.

The gods praised her, and she promised that whenever the world was in trouble she would return. That promise is the heart of the festival.
stories.moral: A wrong that seems unbeatable is usually unbeatable only because nobody considered the obvious answer.
stories.sourceNote: Devi Mahatmya, chapters 2–4 (Markandeya Purana 82–84). Available in full in the Scripture section.

stories.title: The Nine Forms of Maa Durga
stories.short: Navratri means nine nights, and each night has its own form of the Goddess. First comes Shailaputri, the mountain's daughter, steady as a hill. Then Brahmacharini, who practises and practises. Then Chandraghanta, with a bell on her forehead that warns off harm. Then Kushmanda, whose smile was warm enough to make the world. Then Skandamata, holding her baby. Then Katyayani, who fights for what is fair. Then Kalaratri, who is dark and frightening and protects you anyway. Then Mahagauri, shining white after being washed clean. And last Siddhidatri, who gives the fruit of all the practice.
stories.long:
Navratri is nine nights, and the tradition gives each night a form of the Goddess. The list is old: it appears in the Devi Kavacham, which is recited before the Saptashati itself.

Day 1 — Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain. She rides a bull and carries a trident and a lotus. She is about being grounded.

Day 2 — Brahmacharini, the one who practises. She is barefoot, with prayer beads and a water pot. She is about discipline.

Day 3 — Chandraghanta, with a half-moon bell on her forehead. Its sound frightens away harm and comforts the seeker. She is about courage.

Day 4 — Kushmanda, whose warmth made the cosmic egg. Eight arms, riding a lion. She is about creativity.

Day 5 — Skandamata, holding the baby Skanda on her lap. She is about nurture.

Day 6 — Katyayani, the warrior, born from a sage's prayers. She is about justice.

Day 7 — Kalaratri, dark and fearsome, riding a donkey — but with two hands always open in blessing. She is about facing the dark.

Day 8 — Mahagauri, radiant white after being washed in the Ganga. She is about renewal.

Day 9 — Siddhidatri, who gives the fruit of the practice. She is about fulfilment.

Read together the nine days make a journey: from being grounded, through discipline, courage, creativity, nurture, resolve and fearlessness, to purity and fulfilment.
stories.moral: Growth has an order, and you cannot skip to the last step.
stories.sourceNote: Devi Kavacham verses 3–5 (the nine names); the Navadurga Stotram (traditional). Colours and offerings vary by region.

stories.title: Raktabija and the Drop of Blood
stories.short: There was a demon called Raktabija. He had a strange power: every time a drop of his blood touched the ground, a new Raktabija stood up. The Goddess fought him and wounded him, and suddenly there were two of him. She wounded him again, and there were a hundred. The more she fought in the ordinary way, the worse it got. Then Kali came out of the Goddess's forehead. She stretched out her tongue over the battlefield and drank every drop of blood before it could land. With no drops falling, Raktabija could not multiply, and he was defeated. The story is about problems that get bigger when you attack them the ordinary way.
stories.long:
In the Uttama Charitra of the Devi Mahatmya, the brothers Shumbha and Nishumbha send their best warriors against the Goddess one after another. Dhumralochana is destroyed by her mere 'hum'. Chanda and Munda are brought to her by Kali, who arises from Chandika's brow — and from that episode she is called Chamunda.

Then comes Raktabija. His boon was that every drop of his blood that fell on the ground would produce a warrior identical to him.

The battle goes badly in a specific way. The Goddess wounds him, and the army doubles. She wounds him harder, and it doubles again. The text describes the field filling with Raktabijas. Ordinary force is not merely insufficient; it is counterproductive.

The solution is Kali. She spreads herself over the battlefield and catches every drop in her mouth before it reaches the earth. With the multiplication stopped, the original Raktabija can be destroyed.

The episode is one of the most commented-on in the text. It is usually read as a statement about a class of problem — craving, anger, a wrong that reproduces itself — which cannot be cut down directly, because cutting it down is how it spreads. It needs to be met at the point where it would take root.
stories.moral: Some problems grow when you attack them. They have to be met before they land.
stories.sourceNote: Devi Mahatmya chapter 8 (Markandeya Purana 88). Available in full in Scripture.

stories.title: Why She Has So Many Arms
stories.short: If you look at a picture of Durga, you will notice she has many arms — sometimes eight, sometimes ten, sometimes more. It is not to look frightening. It is to show that she can hold many things at once. A sword in one hand, a lotus in another, a drum, a conch, a shield. And notice this: two of her hands are almost always free. One says 'do not be afraid'. The other says 'here is what you need'. And the lion? The lion is fear. She does not kill it. She rides it.
stories.long:
Hindu images are not portraits. They are diagrams — they are trying to show you something that a normal body could not show.

When Durga has eight or ten arms, the image is saying: this being can hold many things at the same time. A trident for balance. A discus for the turning of time. A conch to sound the beginning. A sword to cut one thing away from another. A bow to reach something far away. A lotus to hold the world without being dirtied by it.

The weapons are not all hers originally. In the Devi Mahatmya, each god gives her his own weapon. So the image is also saying: she is what happens when everyone contributes what they are best at.

Then look at her hands again. In almost every picture, two hands are doing something other than fighting. One is raised with the palm outward — that gesture is called abhaya mudra, and it means 'do not be afraid'. The other is turned down, open — varada mudra, 'I am giving'.

So the whole picture says: enormous power, and two hands permanently reserved for reassurance and generosity.

And the lion. In some regions it is a tiger. Either way it stands for fear and appetite. She does not kill it and she does not run from it. She rides it. That is the whole lesson in one image: you do not get rid of fear. You learn to drive.
stories.moral: Strength is not having nothing to fear. It is having your fear underneath you instead of in front of you.
stories.sourceNote: Iconographic reading, informed by the Devi Mahatmya ch. 2 (the gods' weapons). Symbolic interpretations vary between traditions.

stories.title: The King, the Merchant, and the Goddess
stories.short: A king called Suratha lost his kingdom. His own ministers took it. A merchant called Samadhi lost his wealth. His own sons threw him out. Both of them ended up in the same forest, at the same hermitage. And both of them had the same problem: they still loved the people who had ruined them. The king kept worrying about whether his elephant was being fed. The merchant kept wondering if his sons were eating. They went to the sage Medhas and asked the obvious question: why do we still care about people who used us? His answer was the whole Devi Mahatmya — the story of the Goddess, who is also the power that makes us attached. At the end she gave each of them a boon.
stories.long:
The Devi Mahatmya is told inside a frame story, and the frame is the reason the text exists.

Sage Markandeya is speaking to his disciple. The story he tells begins with Suratha, a king who ruled well and was nevertheless defeated by his own ministers, stripped of his treasury, and driven out. Riding alone into the forest, he finds the hermitage of the sage Medhas.

There he meets Samadhi, a wealthy merchant whose wife and sons threw him out once they had his money.

Both men are miserable, but not in the simple way. Suratha knows his ministers are thieves and still cannot stop worrying about them. Samadhi knows his family used him and still aches for them. They ask Medhas the real question: why is our mind attached to people we know have harmed us? Is this our fault, or is something doing this to us?

Medhas answers: this is Mahamaya, the Goddess herself, who deludes all beings — including Brahma and Vishnu. And then, to explain her, he tells the whole story of the Devi Mahatmya: Madhu and Kaitabha, Mahishasura, Shumbha and Nishumbha.

At the end, in chapter 13, both men receive boons. Suratha asks for his kingdom back and for a greater one in the future. Samadhi asks for knowledge — for the removal of the very attachment that brought him there.

The text gives both boons without ranking them. That is worth sitting with.
stories.moral: Attachment is not a personal failing; it is a power in the world, and it can be understood.
stories.sourceNote: Devi Mahatmya chapters 1 and 13 (Markandeya Purana 81 and 93). Available in full in Scripture.
